concepts.name: Constitutional Position and Status of CAG
key_dimensions: Article 148: appointment, oath, and conditions of service
CAG as a constitutional (not statutory) body — significance of this distinction
Comparison with other constitutional authorities (UPSC, Election Commission) in terms of independence safeguards
Why CAG is considered a 'guardian of public purse' — doctrinal basis

concepts.name: Appointment and Removal of CAG
key_dimensions: Appointed by President under his hand and seal — no parliamentary confirmation unlike some democracies
Removal procedure: same as a Supreme Court judge (Article 148(1)) — address by both Houses, special majority
Grounds for removal: proved misbehaviour or incapacity — narrow grounds ensuring security of tenure
UPSC trap: CAG vs. CVC vs. CEC removal procedures — which requires special majority, which does not

concepts.name: Independence Safeguards of CAG
key_dimensions: Salary charged to Consolidated Fund of India — not subject to vote of Parliament
Ineligibility for further office under Union or State after retirement (Article 148(4)) — prevents post-retirement influence
Service conditions cannot be varied to CAG's disadvantage after appointment (Article 148(3))
Comparison trap: CAG vs. Attorney General — AG can appear against government, but CAG cannot hold further office; how do these differ in independence design?

concepts.name: CAG's Audit Jurisdiction: Union Accounts
key_dimensions: Audits accounts of Union government — all ministries and departments
Distinction between 'appropriation audit' (whether money spent on sanctioned head) and 'propriety audit' (whether expenditure was wise and prudent)
Compliance audit vs. performance audit — CAG's expanding mandate
Receipts audit: CAG audits tax and non-tax revenues, not just expenditure — often overlooked

concepts.name: CAG's Audit Jurisdiction: State Accounts
key_dimensions: Article 149 read with CAG's (DPC) Act 1971 — CAG audits state accounts
Dual role: auditor of both Union and States — federal audit architecture
State governments cannot appoint their own auditor general independently — centralised audit design and its federal implications
Trap: CAG audits state accounts but reports go to Governor, not President — Article 151(2)

concepts.name: CAG and Audit of Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs)
key_dimensions: Government companies under Companies Act audited by CAG as supplementary auditor (not primary auditor) — distinction with departmental undertakings
Departmental undertakings (Railways, Defence, Posts) audited directly by CAG as primary auditor
Statutory corporations: depends on individual statute — some fall under CAG, some do not (e.g., RBI does NOT fall under CAG audit)
UPSC trap: Which bodies are NOT audited by CAG? (e.g., RBI, bodies funded entirely by private sources)

concepts.name: CAG and Audit of Autonomous Bodies / NGOs
key_dimensions: Bodies substantially funded by government grants (>75% or ₹1 crore threshold historically) come under CAG's audit
Expanding jurisdiction to societies, trusts, and NGOs receiving government funds — policy and legal basis
CAG's jurisdiction vs. internal audit mechanisms of autonomous bodies
Controversy: CAG seeking to audit political parties receiving government benefits — constitutional and legal limits

concepts.name: CAG and Comptroller Function: The Misnomer Debate
key_dimensions: In India, CAG does NOT exercise 'comptroller' function — cannot withhold funds or pre-audit expenditure
In UK, Comptroller role means prior sanction before government draws from Consolidated Fund — India's CAG lacks this power
CAG is purely a post-facto auditor in India — significance for financial accountability
Why this distinction matters: UPSC frequently tests whether CAG can prevent illegal expenditure in advance

concepts.name: CAG's Reports and Their Submission
key_dimensions: Article 151: CAG submits reports to President (Union) and Governor (States) — who then lay them before legislature
Three types of audit reports: Finance Accounts, Appropriation Accounts, and Audit Reports on receipts/expenditure
CAG does not submit reports directly to Parliament — goes through President/Governor; trap on who 'lays' reports
Timing and frequency of reports — CAG can submit multiple reports in a year, not bound to annual single report

concepts.name: Public Accounts Committee (PAC) and CAG Nexus
key_dimensions: CAG's reports are examined by PAC — symbiotic relationship: CAG is 'friend, philosopher, and guide' of PAC
PAC: composition (22 members, 15 Lok Sabha + 7 Rajya Sabha), chaired by Opposition member by convention
CAG's report triggers PAC examination — but CAG has no enforcement power; PAC provides political accountability
Distinction: PAC vs. Estimates Committee vs. Committee on Public Undertakings — which uses CAG reports?

concepts.name: CAG and Consolidated Fund vs. Contingency Fund vs. Public Account
key_dimensions: CAG audits all three funds but with different degrees of scrutiny — Public Account is significant but often missed
Public Account: moneys held in trust (PF, small savings) — CAG audits these even though not 'government money' per se
Contingency Fund: advances to meet unforeseen expenditure, later regularised by Parliament — CAG's role in regularisation audit
Trap: Contingency Fund is at disposal of President/Governor — does CAG audit it? Yes, post-facto

concepts.name: Performance Audit and Value-for-Money Audit by CAG
key_dimensions: CAG has expanded from traditional compliance/regularity audit to '3E' audit: Economy, Efficiency, Effectiveness
High-profile performance audits: 2G spectrum, Coalgate, Commonwealth Games — how CAG's findings triggered political crises
Legal basis for performance audit: CAG's DPC Act 1971 — Section 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18 defining audit scope
Criticism: CAG overstepping into policy domain when conducting performance audits — judicial and executive pushback

concepts.name: CAG's Role in Defence Audit
key_dimensions: CAG audits defence services — Army, Navy, Air Force — as they are departmental undertakings
Sensitive nature of defence audit: classified information and CAG's special protocols
CAG's reports on defence procurement irregularities (e.g., Bofors, Rafale controversy — CAG report on Rafale and its methodology questioned)
Trap: Ordnance factories, DRDO — do they fall under CAG? Yes, as they receive government funding

concepts.name: CAG and Local Bodies / Panchayati Raj Institutions
key_dimensions: 73rd and 74th Amendments: State Finance Commissions and audit of PRIs/ULBs — role of CAG
Article 243J and 243Z: Legislature of a State may by law make provisions for maintenance of accounts and their audit for PRIs and ULBs respectively
CAG empowered to audit accounts of PRIs/ULBs — but this is discretionary/state-law dependent, not automatic
Significance for UPSC: CAG's audit of gram panchayats receiving funds under MGNREGA — accountability chain

concepts.name: CAG and the Consolidated Fund: Drawing and Disbursement
key_dimensions: Distinction between 'charged' expenditure (not voted, e.g., CAG's own salary) and 'voted' expenditure — CAG audits both
CAG's own establishment is charged to CFI — institutional independence implication
Parliament cannot reduce CAG's salary/allowances — what happens if Parliament tries to do so indirectly?
Comparison: other bodies whose salaries are charged to CFI (President, Judges, Speaker) — pattern of independence

concepts.name: CAG vs. Internal Audit Mechanisms
key_dimensions: CAG is external/supreme audit institution — distinct from internal audit conducted by ministries (e.g., CGA — Controller General of Accounts)
CGA vs. CAG: CGA (under Finance Ministry) prepares accounts; CAG audits them — separation of accounting and auditing
Pre-2005 position: CAG both compiled and audited accounts — post-separation, only audits
UPSC trap: Who maintains accounts of Union Government? CGA, not CAG — common confusion

concepts.name: CAG's Jurisdiction: Exclusions and Limitations
key_dimensions: CAG cannot audit RBI, SEBI (statutory bodies with own audit under their acts) — important exclusions
CAG cannot conduct real-time or concurrent audit as a constitutional right — only post-facto
Private companies where government holds minority stake not automatically under CAG audit

Trap: Supreme Court in various judgments on CAG's jurisdiction — what did court say about CAG auditing private entities in PPP projects? (CAG can audit concessionaire accounts if government money is involved)

concepts.name: CAG and Public-Private Partnership (PPP) Audit
key_dimensions: Emerging frontier: CAG seeking to audit private parties in PPP concessions where public money/assets are involved
Legal controversy: private companies resisting CAG audit citing Companies Act and contract terms
CAG's position backed by Supreme Court in some cases — basis being 'public interest' and 'public funds' flow
Policy implication: If CAG cannot audit PPPs, large public resources escape accountability — ongoing reform debate

concepts.name: CAG as Supreme Audit Institution (SAI): International Dimension
key_dimensions: INTOSAI (International Organisation of Supreme Audit Institutions) — CAG of India is a member; Lima Declaration principles
ASOSAI: Asian regional grouping — India's leadership role
ISSAI (International Standards of Supreme Audit Institutions) — CAG aligns audit standards with ISSAI
Comparison: UK's National Audit Office (NAO) vs. India's CAG — NAO is statutory, India's CAG is constitutional; different models of independence

concepts.name: High-Profile CAG Reports and Constitutional Implications
key_dimensions: 2G Spectrum Audit Report (2010): CAG estimated notional loss of ₹1.76 lakh crore — methodology controversy and Supreme Court's reliance on it in cancelling licences
Coalgate Report: CAG on coal block allocation — led to Supreme Court cancellation of 214 coal blocks
These cases raise: Can courts use CAG reports as evidence? What is the legal status of CAG reports?
Rafale CAG Report controversy: redacted report, parliamentary privilege, and scope of CAG's audit of defence deals — systemic implications
